region.zh: 所羅門群島佛羅里達（恩格拉）島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Rev. A. Penny at Florida, printed in R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A heron with his foot fast in the coral called every fish that passed — shark, bonito, garfish, rock-cod, crocodile — and every one said 'Wait a bit.' Only the turtle agreed to help, for pay: the sea-urchin beside the heron. Freed, the heron repaid his debt by dancing the children away from their prize and singing the turtle out of the net and into the sea.
summary.zh: 蒼鷺足陷珊瑚，潮水漸沒其頸。他向過路諸魚求救——鯊、鰹、長嘴魚、石斑、鱷——皆答『且等等』。唯海龜索酬而助之，蒼鷺身旁的海膽恰可為酬；龜食海膽大喜，碎石化石救出蒼鷺，並結生死之盟。後 Hagelonga 村捕得海龜，備宴待宰；蒼鷺翩然而至，向村童借得父母最貴之飾物，為其起舞，趁機歌咒解縛：『Kerembaembae！縛解矣……』一路舞咒，送龜潛入海中。村人追悔，見沙上龜跡，方知龜自行得脫。

sensitivity.note: Native-language text taken down by Rev. A. Penny at Florida; translated by Codrington (1891). Gela heritage.

passages.text: One day a Soo, a heron, caught his foot fast in the coral; the tide came in, but his neck was long. When the tide reached to the top of his neck there came along a Shark. 'Come and save me,' says the Soo. 'Wait a bit,' says the Shark. There comes a bonito: 'Come and save my life,' says the Soo; and the bonito says to him, 'Wait a bit.' There comes the great Garfish: 'Come and save me, brother,' says the Soo; the Garfish says, 'Wait a bit.' There comes a Rock-cod: 'Come and save my life,' says the Soo; 'Wait a bit,' says the Rock-cod. There comes a Crocodile: 'Come and save me,' says the Soo; 'Wait a bit,' says the Crocodile. In the end all the fish came, and nothing could be done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then comes a Turtle. 'Brother! come here and save my life,' says the Soo. And the Turtle says, 'You will pay me of course.' And the Soo says, 'I have nothing with me to pay you with.' And there was a sea-urchin alongside the Soo, and he says, 'I will pay you with money,' says he. But the Turtle says, No. And the Soo says, 'Dog's teeth, and porpoise teeth'; but the Turtle says, 'No, I don't want it.' Then he offers him the sea-urchin, and the Turtle eats it up with great delight, and says joyfully, 'Now I will save you, you have given me my pay.' So he smashes to fragments the stone that held the bird's foot and the Soo is saved. And the Soo says, 'Now you have saved my life; if ever hereafter you are going to be killed and I should hear you call, I will come and save you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.

passages.text: After this the people of Hagelonga went to fish, and let down their net; every fish that passed they let go, but the turtle that came round they cried out over, 'Here he is! we will see what he is worth,' and took him, and tied him, and carried him ashore, and made a fence round him. The chief of Hagelonga says, 'To-morrow we will split wood for him, and get leaves, and dig yams for him, this turtle of ours.' So as soon as it was light they went off; and when they were far away the Soo comes along, and the boys watching say to him, 'Where have you come from?' and the Soo says, 'I am just idling about; should you like me to dance for you?' And he says, 'Bring me the porpoise teeth and dog's teeth ornaments of your fathers and mothers, that I may dress myself up in the best.' And he dressed himself out in them, and then he danced for them — dancing along to the fence in which the Turtle was. And the Turtle saw him coming, and cried out, 'Now I am to die, my brother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the Soo says to him, 'And now I shall save your life, because you saved mine before.' And he came into the house where the boys were, and there he danced for them, singing 'Kerembaembae! Loosed is your leg that they have tied!' — and his leg is loosed. 'Kerembaembae! Slipped out is your head! Clear the forepart! Clear the hinder part! Clear the rest of you!' — and so it was. 'Kerembaembae! Follow the path! Reach the sand! Down with you into the sea! Dive out of sight! Go a fathom's length! Go two fathoms!' So he escaped with his life. And the people returned and looked at the fence, but the Soo was gone; and they said, 'Some one has stolen our turtle.' And the boys said, 'There was only a Soo came here and danced for us, and we gave him all your things, and he deceived us.' And they went and looked at the path, and there they saw the traces of the turtle, and they said, 'Yea, he has saved himself for certain, nobody has stolen him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島烏雷帕拉帕拉島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The box-fish Watwata and the sole scratched each other by turns, each leaving the other worse; then they played hide-and-seek. The sole buried himself in the sand where the Watwata could not find him — and the Song-fish, who stood laughing at the game, has grinned ever since.
summary.zh: 箱魚瓦瓦塔與比目魚互抓對方，一抓比一抓狠：比目魚抓得箱魚遍體，箱魚回敬竟把比目魚抓得極薄。二人於是玩捉迷藏：箱魚藏於石下被找到；比目魚埋身沙中，箱魚遍尋不著。一旁露齒的松魚看了大笑——牠至今還咧著嘴笑。

passages.text: The story of the Watwata (an Ostracion) and the Sole. The two were scratching one another, and the Sole said to the Watwata, 'Scratch me.' But the Watwata said, 'No, you shall scratch me first.' And the Sole scratched the Watwata, scratched him well. And the Watwata said, 'Brother, you have scratched me badly,' but the Sole said, 'No, it is all right.' And the Watwata said, 'Well! now I shall scratch you in my turn.' After that he scratched him, scratched him extremely thin. And the Sole said, 'Well! you have scratched me badly, but we two will play hide and seek.' And the Sole said, 'You shall hide first.' After that the Watwata hid, and got out of sight under a stone. The Sole sought him and found him. After that the Sole hid in his turn, and buried himself in the sand; and the Watwata sought him in vain. But the Song (a fish which shews its teeth) stood and laughed at it; and he has grinned so ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birds' Voyage in the Arum-Leaf Canoe

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native Mota manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The birds set out in a canoe of a giant arum leaf to eat the tawan fruit of Qakea, taking aboard every would-be passenger who sang 'I go and tell my daddy!' — even the hermit crab. But the crab's claw pierced the leafy hull; all leapt overboard and swam ashore while the crab sank and crawled along the bottom; the Weru dived till her body turned black and her eyes red in search of him — and the crab was already sitting quietly on the sand. Afterwards, in pairs, the birds tidied each other's feathers, and the Rat, combing the Owl's head with 'comb-comb-dung-dung,' defiled him; the betrayed Owl roasted a red-raia caladium to lure the Rat from his hole and killed him with his talons.
summary.zh: 群鳥以巨芋葉為舟，乘風往 Qakea 食塔萬果。綠鸚鵡、鸚嘴、鴿先後求搭船，皆唱『我要告訴爸爸去！風吹得你們夠嗆』而得上船；寄居蟹也想同行，眾鳥本以『你留下看島』拒之，被其『你們吃落果、我在地上撿』說動而載之。白鸛叮嘱：『莫亂動，別把舟抓破。』蟹爪終究把芋葉舟抓穿，海水灌入。眾鳥跳海游泳登岸，蟹沉底爬行；白鸛潛水尋蟹，尋到身黑眼紅——而蟹早已安坐沙灘。眾鳥成對互相理羽；鼠替貓頭鷹梳頭，口中念『梳梳—拉屎—拉屎』，竟在鷹頭上拉屎。鸚鵡告密，鷹怒而追鼠；鼠鑽洞不出。鷹烤紅薯達至香氣入洞，置其洞口，待鼠出而搏殺食之。

sensitivity.note: Native Mota manuscript translated by Codrington (1891).

passages.text: They lived in their place. The tattan was in fruit at Qakea; the wind began to blow; then said they, 'Well, now at last we will paddle over and eat tawan.' So they make a start and go. And the reitga, the Green Parrot, says, 'I go with you'; but they say, 'O-o-o! You just go back, lest your father should be angry with us about you.' And he sings, 'I go and tell my daddy! the wind has blown hard against you; beat, beat!' 'Ah, well! come along!' and he gets on board. Then the Mes and the Pigeon in turn ask to come, and sing the same song; and each gets on board. And when all were on board there was a Hermit Crab sitting there, and he said, 'You fellows, just let me come.' But they said, 'You just stay there to look after our island.' And he said, 'Nay, my brothers, you won't make me miserable. Take me over! I will sit under the tawan-trees, and you will eat making the fruit fall, and I will eat on the ground.' So they said, 'Very well! come along'; and he gets on board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Weru says to the Crab, 'Friend, sit up this way near me; and while we two are sitting here, don't shuffle about, lest you make a hole in the canoe' — for the canoe was the leaf of a giant arum. And he says, 'Yes, I know all about that.' But the Weru keeps an eye upon him, and if he shuffles with his claws she says to him, 'Friend, I keep telling you, don't be shuffling about; eh! you will soon have made a hole in the canoe!' But he says, 'Eh! Friend, I know all about it.' The wind had come down into their sail, and they were already in the open sea; and the Crab shuffled about, and his claw pierced right through the canoe, and the water came pouring quickly in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And they cried out, 'Be quick! our canoe has a hole in it, the Crab had trodden it through.' And they said, 'Well, let us leap overboard'; and they all of them leapt overboard, and the Crab leapt overboard, and sank right out of sight to the bottom of the sea; but they all of them swam, and he crawled along on the bottom. And they all swam and came out upon the shore, but not he you may be sure. Then they said, 'Fellows! are we all men alive or not?' And some one said, 'No, there is one poor fellow our friend missing.' And they spoke to one, and he refused, and to another, and he refused; then said the Weru, 'Here am I, I will go and look for him.' So she swims, and dives, and does not find him, and comes up to the surface; and dives again, and goes on diving, and her body turns black, and dives, and dives, and her eyes turn red. But the Crab had already crawled up ashore before them all; and there he was quietly sitting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then said the Tasis to the Tagere, 'Friend, come here and make me tidy'; and they all of them sat down in pairs. Then said the Rat to the Owl, 'Friend, come here, let me make you tidy'; and as he combs his head he keeps saying, 'Comb-comb-dung-dung'; and he dungs upon the head of the Owl. Then says the Rat, 'My paws are tired out.' The Mes parrot combs the Owl's head, and perceives that it smells, and cries out; and the Parrot says, 'Oh! your friend the Rat has played you a trick; he has made a pig of himself upon you.' Then the Owl flies off and chases the Rat; and the Rat saw a hole and ran into it, and the Owl sat by helpless. Then he roasts a red raia caladium, and as he scrapes that root the smell goes out and reaches the Rat in the hole; and when it was cooked he broke it and put it at the mouth of the hole. Then the Rat creeps out to eat, and the Owl swooped down upon him, and killed him with his talons, and ate him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The Shark quarrelled with the Snake and bade him come down into the sea to be eaten. The Snake answered, 'They will kill you, and I shall eat a bit of you.' And so it fell out: when the Shark was killed, the Snake went down into the sea and ate the Shark.
summary.zh: 鯊與蛇結怨，鯊令蛇下海，欲食之。蛇答曰：『人們會殺了你，而我要吃你一口。』後果然：人們殺鯊之時，蛇下海把鯊吃了。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: This is about the Shark and the Snake. They quarrelled, and the Shark told the Snake to come down into the sea, that the Shark might eat him. The Snake said to him, 'They will kill you, and I shall eat a bit of you.' Now when they killed the Shark, the Snake went down into the sea and ate the Shark — the small talker proved the surer prophet, and the boastful biter ended inside the belly he had threatened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: Kamakajaku Swallowed by the King-Fish, Guest of the Sun
title.zh: 卡馬卡雅庫：鯖魚吞身、日宮作客

region.en: Gaji hill, Bugotu, Ysabel, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島伊莎貝爾島布戈圖加吉山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Kamakajaku of Gaji hill waded far out to dip salt-water as dark as the sea he had watched, and was swallowed by a great king-fish and carried east to the rising of the sun. He cut his way out with the obsidian in his ear, followed the Sun to his village, taught his fireless hosts cooked food, disobeyed their taboo and looked down the sky-hole at his own home — and was lowered back by canes, reaching the hill of Gaji to die there old.
summary.zh: 加吉山上的卡馬卡雅庫見海上奇黑，令孫兒取水來比，不似；親自下海，遠涉至能望見山處取水，水面轟鳴，一條巨鯖把他吞下，向日出之東游去。至淺灘，他取出耳中所藏之黑曜石割破魚肚躍出。旭日升起，滾滾而行，囑他『別擋路，站我右邊』。他隨日上天，至太陽兒孫之村作客；彼輩只食生冷，他教他們用火熟食。主人告誡一處禁地不可去；他忍不住，掀開蓋天石孔，俯見故里加吉，放聲大哭。主人乃以竹竿縛籃縋他下天，囑他『鳥獸齊鳴時莫抬頭，待地上蟬鳴再望』。竹竿接了一根又一根，直垂至加吉山。親友本以為他已死，見他自天而降，皆大歡喜。他活到高壽，終老於加吉山上。

sensitivity.note: Native Bugotu manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Ysabel heritage.

passages.text: He dwelt upon the hill at Gaji; and he was mending his nets, and he looked down upon the ocean, and saw it dark exceedingly. And his grandchildren went down to the sea to fish upon the reef, and Kamakajaku said to them, 'Go and dip salt-water for me in the place I see the sea like that.' And his grandchildren went forth and dipped the salt-water, and came up and gave it to him. And he poured it down, and looked and did not find it like what he looked down upon from his place upon the hill. And it was morning, and he took the salt-water-vessel, and went forth down, and put in his ear a bit of obsidian, and waded far out from the shore till he saw the hill at Gaji, and then he dipped. And the surface of the sea sounded and bubbled, and he heard coming-to-him a Kombili, a king-fish, a very great fish; and it came and swallowed him, and went off with him eastwards to the lining up of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it went with him till it arrived with him at a shallow place, and it threw itself about so that Kamakajaku perceived that there was a beach probably. 'Here am I,' says he, and he thought of the obsidian in his ear, and felt for it and found it, and cut asunder the belly of the Kombili, and leapt out, and saw a brightness. So up rose the Sun with a tang, and rolling from side to side. And the Sun says, 'Don't stand in my way, you will die at once; stay on my right.' And he drew aside till the Sun rose away, and then he followed; and they two went up towards heaven, and went on and arrived at the village of the Sun's children. And he said, 'Here you stay'; so he stayed with them, with his children and grandchildren, and the Sun went off. And they asked him, 'Whence did you come hither?' And he said, 'From the earth; I dwelt in my place, and I dipped salt-water, and a big fish swallowed me, and so I arrived here at your good town.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: So they remained in company; and they ate only raw food, those people above; and he shewed them fire, so that they ate cooked food. And they said to him, 'Don't go to that place, it is taboo'; and they went their way. And he kept house, and thought what that was they had said, and went over, and opened up a stone which was the covering of a hole in the sky, and he looked down on his place at Gaji, and he cried. They brought him food, but it was not for him; so they asked him, 'Do you want to go down?' And he said, Yes. And they made a house, and gave him a banana, and gave him seed of pan to dye with, and they took a cane and tied it to the saddle-piece of the house, and he Kamakajaku sat in it. And they let it down, saying, 'When the birds cry, don't look out; when the cicalas cry, then you may look out.' And when one cane was too short, they tied another to it, and it reached down to the hill and rested.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And his friends had been seeking him, because they thought that he was dead already. And on the day that he came down again from heaven, they rejoiced because they saw him again, and good was their heart. And he lived a long while, till he died on his hill Gaji — the man who went up with the Sun, and came down again by a rope of canes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: Samuku Sent to the Ghosts' Mangroves

region.en: Tuhilagi, Bugotu, Ysabel, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島伊莎貝爾島布戈圖圖希拉吉鬼沼（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Scolded by his wife — 'your father and mother are dead, who is to make you food? Go and see them in Tuhilagi' — Samuku paddled to the Ghosts' Mangroves and found the company of ghosts, who told him he was not dead yet. Their house vanished at dawn; he netted their fishing and saw their true forms; and when the ghost company left him at daybreak, the people of a certain place found him sleeping on the sand and took him in till he died.
summary.zh: 薩穆庫勤耕娶妻，家和食足。一日歸家索食，妻怒罵：『我厭倦為你備食；你父母已死，誰給你做飯？去圖希拉吉看他們去吧。』他負氣駕舟至鬼沼 Lelegia tarunga，登上鬼群之鄉。眾鬼問：『你還沒死，怎麼來了？』他答：『我妻罵我，把我趕來的。』夜宿鬼舍，天明屋竟消失。他設計織網與眾鬼下海捕魚，看清了鬼的真形；天亮鬼群散去，他睡在沙灘上，被附近村人拾回，供養至死。

sensitivity.note: Native Bugotu manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Ysabel heritage.

passages.text: Samuku lived in his village, and built his house, and worked, and good and many were his affairs; so he took a wife and married, and they two lived well, and agreed perfectly well together, and worked, and much was their food. And Samuku came home and asked for food, because he was hungry, and his wife had not prepared any food, and Samuku was angry with his wife, and scolded her greatly. And his wife said to him, 'I am tired of making food for you, your father and mother are dead, who is to make you food? Go and see them in Tuhilagi.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Samuku was angry, and he sat and thought; and he said, 'Good, I will go and see them.' So he hauled down a canoe and put out to sea to Tuhilagi, and landed at Lelegia tarunga, the Ghosts' Mangroves, and stepped up the beach and went in shore, and found the company of ghosts. And they asked him, 'Why have you come here? You are not dead yet.' And Samuku answered, 'My wife scolded me, and sent me here.' And at night he stayed in a house, and when it was morning the house disappeared. So he played them a trick and made a net, and they went to fish with it, and he saw the forms of the ghosts, and the net caught in the coral. And when it was light all the company of ghosts departed from him, and he went down and slept on the sand. And the people of a certain place found him and took hold of him, and took him to be with them till he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mim People Drag the Yams Through the Islands

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖托雷斯群島（希烏—洛—托加）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The Mim people dragged yams ashore at Hiw and along to Tugua, slicing them in half for the men of each island; where the yams were dragged whole they are very large and long to this day. Only at Lo, where everyone was down on the reefs fishing, did the people hear nothing — and their yams are the small rinds the children later picked from the tree-roots along the path.
summary.zh: 米姆人把薯從希烏島曳至圖瓜，途經各島皆呼人來把薯切半分種；凡整薯拖過之地，其薯至今碩大修長。唯獨洛島之人盡下礁捕魚，無人聽見，事後只在沿路樹根上拾得黏著的薯皮，種而得薯——故洛島之薯不大，卻也足食。米姆人一路喊著『來切薯、替我們分擔』，把薯拖遍群島。

passages.text: They say that the Mim people dragged the yams from place to place, having brought them ashore at Hiw, and then dragged them to Tugua, for which reason the yams at Hiw and at Tugua are very large and long. But when they dragged them along here to Lo, all the people were down on the reefs fishing and heard nothing of it; nor did they know anything till they found the rind of the yams sticking to the roots of the trees along the path. These they picked up and planted; and on that account the Lo yams are not very large, but plentiful enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Because the Mim people sliced their yams in half for the men of Hiw and of Tugua, and then passed on to Toga, and sliced again for them there, on which account the yams there are very large and long. Afterwards they crossed to Ureparapara, where the people sliced the yams in half and planted them. They did the same in all the islands that way; it was only at Lo that the people did not see and hear what was going on. The crowns of the yams remained and were planted somewhere. The Mim people went dragging the yams through all the islands, shouting and calling to the men of every place to come and slice the yams, and take their burden from them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Muesarava and the First Bone-Tipped Arrows
title.zh: 穆埃薩拉瓦與毒骨箭之始

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: In old times there was no fighting. But the blind old man Muesarava shot a pigeon he never saw, and two young men ate it from his oven while he sang. His revenge: he grubbed up a dead boy and ground his bones to arrow-points, which killed where wood and fish-bone could not. When his enemies begged the secret, he told them — and died of their first bone-tipped volley. That first dead man's bone still remains, a fofo arrow full of mana: point it towards a rumoured war, and the fighting comes to nothing.
summary.zh: 上古無戰事。盲叟穆埃薩拉瓦聞鴿啼，張弓亂射竟中鴿；與芋同烤，歌而待食。兩名少年偷開其爐，食盡鴿肉，另烤壞物塞回，遠處唱答。盲叟大怒，圖謀開戰：他以手刨出一座已埋之童屍，取骨磨利製箭；敵方仍以木、魚骨為鏃。開戰後，敵箭中他而不死，他的骨箭中人即斃。敵眾不解，求其法；他直言：『去刨我射死的人，刮其骨為鏃。』敵從其言，再戰，盲叟應聲而亡。那支親手所磨之人骨箭至今猶存，木柄屢換而骨鏃不朽，藏於其兄之弟家中，人以為滿蓄瑪那：若有戰訊，向那方向指之，戰事即消。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage. Records a war-relic cult object.

passages.text: They say that in old times there was no fighting. But there was an old man whose name was Muesarava, who was blind and used to stay doing nothing in the house; and he heard a pigeon calling, and took a bow and broad-headed arrow and went under the tree; and the pigeon let drop a bit of the fruit it was eating, and that blind man shot at a venture into the tree, and hit the pigeon without seeing it. And he took it up, and went and put it into the oven together with the yams, and sat down and sang a song. But two young fellows came along and quietly opened that old man Muesarava's oven, and ate up his pigeon with some of his yams. Then they went to another place, and sang back a song to him; and he heard it, and went back to eat his pigeon, but found when he uncovered the oven that it was eaten up, and that something not good had been put in its place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he was exceeding angry, and plotted a fight against the people of the place whence the two young men had come who had stolen and eaten Muesarava's food. And now Muesarava began to make fighting arrows of men's bones. Muesarava went and grubbed up with his hands a boy who had died, and took his bones, and beat them to splinters and rubbed them sharp. But his enemies on their side knew nothing of that; they only cut wood into shape, or bones of fish or birds, and fixed them in their arrows, while Muesarava on his side prepared men's bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when they fought they shot at him and hit, but he did not die; and he shot them and they could not live, but died outright all of them. So it often happened, and they saw that they died in very great numbers; and they asked Muesarava why it was that they shot him and he did not die, while he shot them and they all of them died. Therefore he told them and said, 'Go and grub up one of the dead men I have shot, and scrape his bones, and point your arrows with that.' Upon this they listened to his counsel and did as he had said to them; and when they fought again they shot him, and he straightway died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And that thing, the dead man's bone that Muesarava ground to a point for himself with his own hand, still remains, and has not yet been spoilt; the reed-shaft has been spoilt and replaced over and over again, but that dead man's bone still remains; I have seen it myself in my brother's possession; it still remains. The people think a great deal of it, thinking that there is supernatural power, mana, in that fofo arrow. If there is heard a rumour of fighting, and that is pointed in the direction whence it comes, the fighting comes to nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro the Little Feeds His Fish

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tagaro-mbiti floated to a sea-rock, fed the rising fish, and sang them a promised meal of toko with coconut sauce. Merambuto overheard the song, stole the canoe, and called with a small copied voice — and the fish rose and were hooked, roasted and eaten. Tagaro followed the footprints, ate his host's 'bad food' claim to nothing, killed him in his house, burnt it, and set the half-eaten fish back in a salt-water pool, where they revived — one side gone, one side left: Tagaro's half-fish, the soles.
summary.zh: 小塔加羅划舟至海上岩畔，不槳自漂，見群魚自舟底湧起，便以手中之食飼之，並許諾：『後日我以椰漿拌托科來餵你們。』次日他唱著歌呼魚——『我的魚呀，無論你們是誰，好小魚，你們的飯來了，椰漿拌的飯來了。』默蘭布托在岸上偷聽，連夜備食，清早劃走小塔加羅之舟，學著喊那歌；只是嗓音太大，魚群不升。他壓低嗓子再唱，魚群盡浮，被他一一釣盡，回村烤食。天明，小塔加羅赴約撲空，循足跡至默蘭布托家，佯坐閒話，問『爐中是什麼？我餓了』；默蘭布托推說『那是我的飯，難吃得很，你吃不下』。小塔加羅道：『那分明是我的魚，叫你釣盡了。』遂擊殺之，焚其屋，把爐中魚取回，放進一小鹹水潭——魚竟復活，只是半邊已失。今人稱之為『塔加羅的半邊魚』——即比目魚。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: They say that he drew down his canoe and paddled out in search of fish; and he saw a great rock standing in the sea, and he floated gently without paddling to see whether he would find fish or not. And he saw many fish rising up to the surface from under his canoe, and he fed them with the food he had in his hand, and he perceived that these fish knew how to eat the food of the land. Then said he, 'I am going to leave you, but the day after to-morrow I shall grate some toko for you to eat, and shall pour cocoa-nut sauce over it, and bring it here to you.' So he left them and stayed, they say, one day at home. And when the second day came for him to go he took that toko which he had sauced with cocoa-nut juice, and launched his canoe, and paddled out to the place where those fish were. And he called them with a song: 'My fish, whatever you are, nice little fish, here is your food with sauce, your food done with cocoa-nut sauce.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: But there was another person, whose name was Merambuto, who stood on the beach, and heard Tagarombiti calling his fish with a song like that, and next day Merambuto, having made haste to prepare food in the night, drew down the canoe in the early morning, Tagarombiti's canoe, and paddled out till he came to the place where Tagarombiti had floated before. And he sang again that song. Then those fish heard his voice that it was loud, and did not rise, because they knew it was a different person by his loud voice. And Merambuto perceived that they did not rise, and he altered his voice so as to be small like Tagarombiti's. And he called them with a small voice singing that song. Then those fish heard that the voice was small, and they rose all of them to the surface, and he caught every one of them with a hook. And he made haste to paddle ashore, and went back into his village, and made up a fire, and put the fish in the oven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: But when it was broad daylight Tagarombiti went himself, and they were all gone; and he understood that this thief Merambuto had caught all the fish, and paddled quickly back and hauled up his canoe. And he looked for footprints to know which way he had gone round; and he found footprints and followed them till he came to Merambuto's place; and there he went into the house to him, and sat down with him in a friendly way. Then said Tagaro, 'What is that in the oven? I am hungry.' And Merambuto said, 'That is my food, but it is very bad, you cannot eat it.' Then says Tagarombiti, 'Indeed is your food so very bad? But those are my fish, and you have caught them all.' And he struck him, and killed him in his house, and set fire to the house, and it was burnt and destroyed. And Tagarombiti took back the fish from the oven, and went back and put them into a little pool of salt-water, and the fish revived; one side of them was gone, one side still remained. And we call them, tavalui tge bulu Tagaro, Tagaro's half-fish — soles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Woman Who Made the Sea

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: An old woman kept her grandson-sons from the fenced ground behind her house, where she made water always into a giant via leaf. While she went to the garden they shot at a lizard sitting on the leaf and burst it — and the water burst forth too. She cried aloud her spell, 'Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!' — and so the sea for the first time stood full around the whole world, for before that they say there was no sea.
summary.zh: 無名老嫗與兩個外孫同居。屋後有一圈葦籬，籬內她獨自使用——那裡放著一片巨大芋葉，她素來就在葉上便溺，並嚴禁二童入內窺看。一日老嫗往園中耕作取食，二兄弟在家射蜥蜴取樂，終於商議：『去看看那禁地是什麼。』他們見到那片芋葉與水；恰有一蜥蜴停在葉上，一童彎弓射之，誤中葉身，葉破水湧。老嫗聞聲，知是二童射破了葉，便立起高聲念咒：『Marodafi bulu, korodafi bulu! Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!』念了三遍——於是海水初次環繞全世界漲滿；據說在此之前世上本無海。老嫗便這樣造出了海。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage. Cross-ref melanesian-baining-tiny-sea (New Britain sea-origin).

passages.text: Nobody knows what her name was, but she was an old woman. And there were two children who lived with her in her house; the story about them is that the mother of these two was the daughter of this old woman. Her house was a good one, fenced about with reeds; there was a fence all round the house, and there was a fence also made against the back of the house, and those two children were forbidden to go into it, because she would be there by herself. And in that little fence at the back of the house she put carefully a leaf of the via, the gigantic caladium; and they say that in that leaf she always made water, and was always very strict in forbidding those two to go there, lest they should see it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And these two were both boys, and they were always shooting lizards. So one day when the old woman went into the garden to work and to bring back food for the three of them, she said to those two, 'Don't you go there!' and they answered, 'Very well, we shall not go.' And she went out of the house, and went into the gardens, and those two brothers played with their bows, shooting lizards. After a while one said to the other, 'It would be a good thing to go and see what it is where the old woman has forbidden us to go.' So they went, and they saw that via leaf and the water in it. Then they saw a lizard sitting on a part of that leaf, and one of them shot at it, but missed the lizard and hit the leaf, and the water that was in it burst quickly forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the old woman heard it, and perceived that those two had probably shot the leaf. And she stood up and cried with a loud voice, 'Marodafi bulu, korodafi bulu! Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!' And thus the sea for the first time stood full around the whole world, for before that they say there was no sea. So the old woman you may say made the sea herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
